title: Remove Duplicate Letters
notes:
Task: Keep one occurrence of every character and minimize the resulting string lexicographically.
Idea: Record each character's last position, then build a stack of chosen characters.
Invariant: The stack has no duplicate characters and preserves the best feasible increasing choice for the processed prefix.
Edge cases: A larger stack-top is removed only if it appears again later, so no required character is lost.
complexity_reason: Each character is pushed and popped at most once; u is the alphabet size in the string.

title: Remove Duplicate Letters
notes:
Task: Return the lexicographically smallest string containing each distinct input letter once.
Idea: Use last-occurrence indices and a stack, removing larger letters when they can safely appear later.
Invariant: Every character in the stack is unique and already selected for the result.
Edge cases: If a character has no later occurrence, it cannot be popped; repeated input letters are skipped once seen.
complexity_reason: Each character enters and leaves the stack at most once.

title: Maximum Product of Word Lengths
notes:
Task: Maximize the product of two word lengths when the words share no letters.
Idea: Encode each word's character set as a 26-bit integer, then test every pair.
Invariant: A pair is compatible exactly when the bitwise AND of its masks is zero.
Edge cases: Duplicate letters set the same bit only once; if no compatible pair exists, the result stays zero.
complexity_reason: Masks are built in one pass over characters and every word pair is checked.

title: Maximum Product of Word Lengths
notes:
Task: Find the largest length product for two words with disjoint letter sets.
Idea: Convert each word into a bitmask and compare all pairs using bitwise AND.
Invariant: A zero mask intersection means the pair shares no lowercase English letter.
Edge cases: Empty or singleton word lists produce zero because there is no eligible pair.
complexity_reason: Mask construction scans all characters and the nested loops test every pair.

title: Bulb Switcher
notes:
Task: Count bulbs left on after n rounds of toggling bulbs whose positions are divisible by the round number.
Idea: Return the integer square root of n.
Invariant: A bulb is toggled once for each divisor; only perfect squares have an odd divisor count.
Edge cases: n<=0 yields zero, and isqrt avoids floating-point rounding.
complexity_reason: Integer square root uses constant auxiliary storage and bounded machine-word work.

title: Bulb Switcher
notes:
Task: Determine how many bulbs remain on after the divisor-based toggling rounds.
Idea: Count perfect squares not exceeding n using floor(sqrt(n)).
Invariant: Bulb i is on precisely when i has an odd number of positive divisors, which happens for squares.
Edge cases: n=0 returns zero; the square root is floored to an integer.
complexity_reason: The method performs one square-root operation and stores no input-sized structure.

title: Coin Change
notes:
Task: Find the minimum number of unlimited coins needed to make amount, or return -1 if impossible.
Idea: Let dp[x] be the fewest coins for amount x and try each denomination as the final coin.
Invariant: After processing x, dp[x] is optimal because every smaller remainder has already been solved.
Edge cases: dp[0]=0; unreachable amounts retain a sentinel larger than any useful count.
complexity_reason: Each amount checks c coin denominations and the DP array has amount+1 entries.

title: Coin Change
notes:
Task: Return the fewest coins needed to form amount with unlimited denominations.
Idea: Build dp[x] from dp[x-coin]+1 for every coin that fits.
Invariant: dp[x] stores the minimum number of coins for every amount already processed.
Edge cases: Amount zero needs zero coins; unreachable amounts are detected by the sentinel value.
complexity_reason: For every amount the algorithm scans all c coin types.

title: Power of Three
notes:
Task: Decide whether n is a power of three.
Idea: Check that n is positive and divides the largest power of three representable in signed 32-bit range.
Invariant: Every positive power of three divides 3^19, while other positive integers cannot divide it evenly.
Edge cases: Zero and negative values are rejected before the divisibility test.
complexity_reason: The method performs a constant number of integer operations.

title: Power of Three
notes:
Task: Test whether an integer is a positive power of three.
Idea: Use divisibility by 3^19, the largest power of three fitting in a signed 32-bit integer.
Invariant: All powers of three in the supported positive integer range divide 1162261467.
Edge cases: n must be positive; negative values and zero return false.
complexity_reason: The implementation uses one positivity check and one remainder operation.

title: Odd Even Linked List
notes:
Task: Group nodes at odd positions before nodes at even positions while preserving order within each group.
Idea: Maintain odd and even tails, advancing each through every other node, then attach the even head after the odd tail.
Invariant: The odd chain contains original odd-position nodes processed so far and the even chain contains original even-position nodes.
Edge cases: Empty and singleton lists are returned unchanged; the judge supplies ListNode.
complexity_reason: Each node is visited a constant number of times and only pointers are stored.

title: Odd Even Linked List
notes:
Task: Rearrange a linked list so odd-indexed nodes precede even-indexed nodes, retaining relative order.
Idea: Split the list into odd and even chains and connect the odd tail to the saved even head.
Invariant: odd and even point to the current tails of their respective original-position chains.
Edge cases: Null and one-node heads need no changes; ListNode is provided by the judge.
complexity_reason: The linked list is traversed once with a constant number of pointers.

title: Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix
notes:
Task: Find the longest orthogonal path whose values strictly increase at every move.
Idea: DFS from each cell and memoize the longest path starting there.
Invariant: memo[r][c] is the optimal increasing path length beginning at cell (r,c).
Edge cases: Strict comparison prevents cycles; empty matrices return zero.
complexity_reason: Each cell is memoized once and checks four neighbors.

title: Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix
notes:
Task: Return the longest path in a matrix that increases strictly with each orthogonal step.
Idea: Memoized DFS computes the best path starting from each cell and considers only larger neighbors.
Invariant: memo[r][c] caches the exact longest increasing path length from that cell.
Edge cases: Strict increase makes the search acyclic; an empty matrix returns zero.
complexity_reason: Every cell's DFS result is cached and each cell checks four neighbors.

title: Verify Preorder Serialization of a Binary Tree
notes:
Task: Validate a preorder serialization where # denotes a null child.
Idea: Start with one slot for the root; each token consumes one slot and each non-null node adds two slots.
Invariant: slots is the number of child positions still available after the processed prefix.
Edge cases: Reject if slots reaches zero before the last token; a valid serialization ends with exactly zero slots.
complexity_reason: The token list and one pass are linear in serialization length.

title: Verify Preorder Serialization of a Binary Tree
notes:
Task: Check whether the comma-separated preorder tokens form a valid binary-tree serialization.
Idea: Count open child slots: a token consumes one, and a non-null node creates two.
Invariant: A valid prefix has a positive slot count until the final token, when it must reach zero.
Edge cases: Early exhaustion or leftover slots makes the serialization invalid.
complexity_reason: Splitting produces O(n) tokens and each token is processed once.

title: Reconstruct Itinerary
notes:
Task: Use every ticket exactly once starting at JFK and choose the lexicographically smallest valid itinerary.
Idea: Store reverse-sorted destinations and run DFS that consumes the smallest remaining edge last in postorder.
Invariant: Each consumed ticket is removed once, and appending airports after exhausting outgoing edges constructs an Eulerian route in reverse.
Edge cases: Multiple tickets between airports remain separate list entries; reverse at the end restores forward order.
complexity_reason: Sorting outgoing ticket lists dominates traversal; each ticket is consumed once.

title: Reconstruct Itinerary
notes:
Task: Reconstruct the lexicographically smallest route from JFK using every ticket once.
Idea: Use a min-heap of destinations per airport and append airports after recursively consuming all outgoing tickets.
Invariant: The postorder list stores the Eulerian itinerary in reverse order once all reachable tickets are consumed.
Edge cases: Priority queues preserve lexical choice when multiple destinations are available; reverse the completed route.
complexity_reason: Each ticket enters and leaves a priority queue once, with logarithmic queue operations.

title: Increasing Triplet Subsequence
notes:
Task: Determine whether three values at increasing indices are strictly increasing.
Idea: Maintain the smallest first value and smallest second value seen; any later value above both completes a triplet.
Invariant: first is the smallest seen candidate for position one, and second is the smallest feasible tail for an increasing pair.
Edge cases: Strict comparisons are required; equal values do not complete the triplet.
complexity_reason: The scan updates two scalar candidates and returns early when a triplet is found.

title: Increasing Triplet Subsequence
notes:
Task: Check whether the array contains a strictly increasing subsequence of length three.
Idea: Keep the smallest first and second values that can end increasing subsequences of lengths one and two.
Invariant: If a value exceeds second, the saved first and second candidates occur earlier and form a valid triplet with it.
Edge cases: Duplicate values update a tail rather than satisfying a strict inequality.
complexity_reason: One pass maintains two values and uses constant extra storage.
